paper.title: CoRe: Combined Rewards with Vision-Language Model Feedback for Preference-Aligned Reinforcement Learning
paper.source_version: arXiv v1, submitted 2026-07-02; versioned PDF SHA-256 624655fd3a8ba0c9049a58f0dce260c749ee9b87a42ef93af33a057e819eee16. Official public code is pinned to default-branch commit d663cabc38e6d6f39ac5e1e4327d94f17f84fa59 (commit date 2026-06-15; no release tag; inspected 2026-08-30). The paper uses Gemini 2.0 Flash, while that code snapshot defaults to Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite.

decision_relevance.why_admitted: CoRe directly constructs a task reward as the clipped sum of executable LLM-generated formal code and a VLM-supervised residual image reward, and it supplies component, feedback-efficiency, alignment-proxy, robustness, and real-robot evaluations. Task text plus start/goal images expose a possible steering interface. Its online relabeling, critic reset, rendering changes, and unequal baseline pretraining also define a sharp boundary for Sam's fixed-trainer experiments.
not_evidence_for: reference selection, motion composition, mode transitions, recovery, phase-window automata, or any reference oracle
human preference calibration or human steering, because CoRe labels preferences with a VLM and reports no human-feedback experiment
a static standalone Python reward, because the residual term requires rendered images, an online learned reward model, preference data, and replay relabeling
reward-only causality under Sam's fixed trainer, because CoRe resets critic state and some baselines use unsupervised pretraining while CoRe does not
statistically resolved superiority, because simulation uses three seeds and the real-robot table reports point estimates without confidence intervals or significance tests
a comparison under Sam's fixed scene and observation contract, because task-specific renderers, cameras, and MetaWorld initial states are modified
portability across a frozen simulator, controller, action interface, dynamics tuple, or training budget
safe execution of generated reward code, immutable reward promotion, or sandboxing
exact reproduction from the README launch path without edits, because the code default VLM and initial-FRM path differ from the paper

mechanisms.name: Formal-plus-residual reward decomposition
mechanisms.description: CoRe forms the policy reward by clipping a code-based formal term and an image-model residual term to [-0.5, 0.5] separately and summing them, assigning explicit task knowledge to FRM and difficult-to-specify visual preference to RRM.

mechanisms.name: Preference-aligned executable formal reward search
mechanisms.description: An LLM proposes executable reward functions from task text, state/action definitions, the previous reward, and policy-component feedback; after the initial task-completion search, candidate segment returns are ranked by agreement with the accumulated VLM preference labels, and only a strict alignment improvement is accepted in the pinned code.

mechanisms.name: Video-preference residual reward learning
mechanisms.description: A VLM compares two trajectory videos against task text and start/goal images, returns a pairwise preference plus per-frame completion weights, and an image reward ensemble learns from preference cross-entropy with a KL penalty toward the interpolated frame-weight distributions; incomparable pairs are excluded.

mechanisms.name: Concurrent reward and policy update loop
mechanisms.description: SAC data collection, policy updates, FRM alignment, VLM querying, and RRM learning proceed online; accepted FRM or RRM updates trigger full replay-buffer relabeling, and the pinned implementation resets the critic when RRM is first enabled.

mechanisms.name: Text-and-image task specification
mechanisms.description: The reward-construction interface consumes task description, state/action definitions, and task start and goal images. This is a potential reward-steering surface, but the paper supplies the inputs once and does not evaluate human correction or a mid-run nudge.

mechanisms.name: Pinned public implementation path
mechanisms.description: The official repository exposes the CoRe trainer, checked-in formal rewards, reward-generation prompts, video-preference labeler, and RRM learner. Its README launch path loads a checked-in initial FRM, later runs preference alignment, defaults to a different Gemini model than the paper, and directly writes and imports generated Python modules.

failure_modes.name: Task-completion reward exploitation
failure_modes.description: Selecting formal rewards solely by task completion can over-weight the nail-position term in Hammer and produce handle-first striking, motivating preference-based candidate selection.

failure_modes.name: Formal-reward expressiveness and label sensitivity
failure_modes.description: The authors report that FRM is limited for deformable objects and sensitive to task difficulty and label noise; Hammer and Fold Cloth show limited improvement under repeated Reward-Preference Alignment.

failure_modes.name: Residual-reward long-horizon feedback limit
failure_modes.description: RRM handles deformable visual tasks better than FRM but struggles on complex long-horizon tasks under limited feedback; the authors attribute residual credit-assignment noise to sparse segment-level supervision.

failure_modes.name: VLM preference and importance noise
failure_modes.description: Only 51.5% of video comparisons agree with task-completion ordering, while 15.0% are wrong and 33.5% abstain; VLM frame weights have only rho=0.48 correlation with progress and yield high variance when used directly as reward.

failure_modes.name: VLM proxy is not human-preference evidence
failure_modes.description: CoRe explicitly operates without humans; preference-label accuracy is evaluated against relative task completion, and no human labeling, inter-rater agreement, preference calibration, or steering experiment substantiates the paper's human-intent language.

failure_modes.name: Fixed-trainer and scene confounds
failure_modes.description: Although policy hyperparameters are common, several baselines receive PEBBLE unsupervised pretraining while CoRe trains directly; CoRe also relabels replay and resets its critic, and the visual reward setup changes render visibility, camera focus, and MetaWorld initial state. The comparison therefore does not isolate a scalar task-reward change under Sam's fixed boundary.

failure_modes.name: FRM ablation prose-table inconsistency
failure_modes.description: Table 2 reports FRM^0 success of 36.0% on Sweep and 34.7% on Dial, then 93.3% and 79.3% for FRM^2. The adjacent prose describes the starts as 30% and assigns the two final values to one alignment, so exact iteration-level attribution should follow the table and retain the discrepancy.

failure_modes.name: Uncertainty and hardware reporting gap
failure_modes.description: Simulation results use three seeds and real-robot results use twenty repetitions, but the reported tables provide no confidence intervals or significance tests. The average wall-clock cost also lacks a hardware specification.

failure_modes.name: Model-query cost, bias, and generalization limits
failure_modes.description: The authors identify iterative LLM/VLM cost, propagation of model bias or inaccuracies, robustness and scalability, and evaluation in more diverse unstructured real environments as unresolved issues; stronger single modules cost roughly 6-9 times more for limited gains in Hammer.

failure_modes.name: Paper-to-code version and launch-path gap
failure_modes.description: The untagged pinned repository defaults to Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite rather than the paper's Gemini 2.0 Flash. Its recommended launch scripts load checked-in initial FRMs instead of rerunning the paper's initial task-completion candidate search, although later preference-alignment updates remain active.

failure_modes.name: Unspecified generated-code execution boundary
failure_modes.description: The pinned implementation extracts LLM output into Python files, dynamically imports candidate functions, and can launch training subprocesses. Neither paper nor repository documents a sandbox, import allowlist, static validator, or immutable review/promotion step.

evaluation.name: Ten-task simulation benchmark
evaluation.description: Seven MetaWorld rigid/articulated tasks use success rate and three SoftGym deformable tasks use episode return; learning curves and final results are averaged over three seeds, with CoRe reporting 99.0% mean MetaWorld success.

evaluation.name: FRM, RRM, importance, and combination ablation
evaluation.description: Ten-task final performance compares FRM at multiple alignment iterations, RRM without importance, RRM with importance, and full CoRe; the combined method is best on every listed task metric in Table 2.

evaluation.name: Preference-quality and reward-progress diagnostics
evaluation.description: The evaluation separates correct, incorrect, and no-preference VLM labels; measures VLM importance weights against task progress; and measures normalized learned-reward correlations along expert trajectories, reporting CoRe rho=0.88.

evaluation.name: Feedback and training-cost accounting
evaluation.description: Tables report labels, images, API tokens, dollars, and wall-clock time. CoRe uses 150-500 labels by task group and averages 2.00M tokens, $0.37, and 2.15 hours per run across ten tasks.

evaluation.name: Five-task UR5 direct-deployment evaluation
evaluation.description: Policies are retrained in task-specific simulations and deployed on UR5 hardware without real-world fine-tuning for Drawer Open, Dial Turn, Hammer, Fold Cloth, and Straighten Rope; each method is repeated twenty times with task-specific success or geometric metrics.

evaluation.name: Model-substitution and visual-disturbance evaluation
evaluation.description: Hammer tests stronger proprietary models, Sweep/Hammer test Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct and Video-LLaVA-7B substitutions, and a moving red-cube distractor tests perceptual robustness on two tasks.

evidence.locator: arXiv v1 record and version history, submitted 2026-07-02
evidence.claim: The active v1 record gives the exact title, authors Hexian Ni, Tao Lu, and Yinghao Cai, arXiv identifier 2607.01721, 2026 date, and ICML 2026 comment.

FRM generates executable reward candidates from task/interface context, the prior best reward, and policy feedback; Reward-Preference Alignment selects the candidate with maximum segment-preference prediction accuracy, replacing task-completion selection that can produce hammer-handle exploitation.

RRM queries a VLM with task text, start/goal images, and two videos for pair preference and per-frame importance; incomparable labels are excluded, and the image reward is trained with preference cross-entropy plus an alpha-weighted KL importance constraint.

The paper uses SAC state policies, GPT-4.1 mini formal rewards, five searches of four candidates, Gemini 2.0 Flash preference labels, uniform queries, interpolated/softmax frame weights, and clipped-and-summed FRM/RRM; some baselines use PEBBLE pretraining, and task-specific rendering is used for reward learning.

The algorithm interleaves off-policy learning, periodic formal reward generation and preference selection, periodic VLM queries and RRM optimization, and full replay relabeling after either reward update.

FRM runs five four-candidate GPT-4.1 mini searches; RRM uses a four-layer CNN for MetaWorld, ResNet-18 for SoftGym, a three-model tanh ensemble, Adam at 3e-4, batch 32 or 8, uniform queries, and MetaWorld segment length 20 downsampled to three VLM frames.
Table 7 reports task-group train and initialization steps, random steps, FRM and VLM periods, per-session query counts, segment sizes, feedback caps, KL weight 5, and reward batches.
Table 8 reports the Fold Cloth and other-task network depths, widths, learning rates, batches, initial temperature, critic target period, Adam betas, discount, and critic EMA tau.
Across seven MetaWorld and three SoftGym tasks run with three seeds, Table 1 reports CoRe's final task results and Section 4.2 reports a 99.0% average MetaWorld success rate.

evidence.locator: Table 2 and Section 4.3, Effects of FRM and RRM / Reward-Preference Alignment
evidence.claim: Ten-task ablations compare FRM iterations, RRM without frame importance, RRM, and combined CoRe; the authors report module limitations and sensitivity to difficulty and label noise. Table 2's Sweep/Dial values differ from the adjacent prose's stated starting values and iteration attribution.

CoRe uses 500 MetaWorld labels and 4,000 images, 150 Fold Cloth labels and 1,200 images, and 200 Rope/Water labels and 1,600 images; the paper describes a 3-40x label reduction relative to selected baselines.

evidence.locator: Table 4 and Section 4.2, average training cost
evidence.claim: A full CoRe run averages 2.00 million tokens, 0.37 US dollars of API cost, and 2.15 wall-clock hours across ten tasks; the table does not state hardware.

Video labels are 51.5% correct, 15.0% incorrect, and 33.5% no-preference against task completion; frame importance has average rho 0.48 and is noisy as a direct reward; learned-reward/task-progress correlations are 0.09, 0.44, 0.48, 0.56, 0.77, and 0.88 from PrefVLM through CoRe.

Five policies retrained in task-specific simulations are directly deployed without fine-tuning on UR5 tasks, repeated twenty times, and evaluated with success or geometric task metrics; Table 5 reports CoRe's results.

evidence.locator: Section 5, Conclusion and Future Work; Impact Statement
evidence.claim: The authors identify iterative LLM/VLM query cost, output bias or inaccuracies, robustness and scalability, and generalization to diverse unstructured real environments as limitations or future work.

Stronger proprietary single-module models add roughly 6-9x API cost for limited Hammer gains; Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct produces results on Sweep/Hammer while Video-LLaVA-7B does not; a moving red-cube distractor reduces CoRe success modestly on two tasks.

evidence.locator: Appendix A, task, observation, action, rendering, camera, and real-robot setup
evidence.claim: The paper specifies task-dependent state/image observations and actions, makes the MetaWorld arm and SoftGym pickers transparent for reward images, changes camera focus and MetaWorld initial states, and reconfigures simulation before real deployment.

evidence.locator: Official repository README lines 24-36 at commit d663cabc38e6d6f39ac5e1e4327d94f17f84fa59
evidence.claim: The official code snapshot configures an RRM VLM and FRM LLM through an OpenAI-compatible API, defaulting to gemini-2.5-flash-lite and gpt-4.1-mini, respectively; no release tag exists at inspection time.

evidence.locator: run_meta.sh lines 1-16 at commit d663cabc38e6d6f39ac5e1e4327d94f17f84fa59 (representative; every published task block in run_meta.sh and run-soft.sh sets the same flag)
evidence.claim: The README-recommended launchers set use_FRM_online=False for the published tasks.

evidence.locator: FRM/reward_code.py lines 138-202 and 322-372 at commit d663cabc38e6d6f39ac5e1e4327d94f17f84fa59
evidence.claim: The release extracts model responses into Python files, imports generated reward functions dynamically, launches initial candidate-training subprocesses, and imports later preference-aligned candidates; no sandbox or static validation contract is documented in these paths.
At RRM activation the public trainer learns RRM, relabels replay, resets the critic, performs reset updates, and then fuses weighted formal and residual rewards for subsequent SAC learning.

evidence.locator: train_CoRe.py lines 145-166 and 314-350 at commit d663cabc38e6d6f39ac5e1e4327d94f17f84fa59
evidence.claim: When use_FRM_online is false, trainer initialization imports a checked-in formal-reward module; the scheduled alignment loop later calls FRM_generate and relabels replay if a candidate improves preference accuracy.
